tier_reason: The gist itself (fast-strlen.c) is the public benchmark, timing libc strlen next to threaded_strlen with the build command (gcc -O3 -march=native ... -lpthread), the compiler version (gcc 13.1.1) and the CPU (Xeon W-2245 @ 3.90GHz) all stated: 43.56 vs 16.84 GB/s, with every variant's returned length asserted equal and printed. The earlier E5-2650 v4 / gcc 9.4.0 block was produced by a version of the code that is not in the gist (it scanned 4.00GB and found length 4000007776, while both revisions set N_BUF to 2e9), so only the W-2245 run is reproducible from published code.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Xeon W-2245 @ 3.90GHz, gcc 13.1.1, 2.00GB buffer scanned 10 times: threaded_strlen 43.56 GB/s (0.46 s) vs libc strlen 16.84 GB/s (1.19 s), about 2.6x (derived from page data). Xeon E5-2650 v4 @ 2.20GHz, gcc 9.4.0, 4.00GB header: 34.09 GB/s (1.17 s) vs 8.76 GB/s (4.56 s), about 3.9x (derived from page data), measured on an unpublished variant of the code. threaded_strlen uses sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN) threads, against single-threaded libc strlen.
corrections.workload: strlen of one posix_memalign'd 2e9-byte buffer filled with 'A' and NUL-terminated at the last byte (length 1999999999), scanned 10 times per variant, with each call's result asserted equal to the first. The E5-2650 v4 block in the header reports a 4.00GB scan with length 4000007776, which does not match N_BUF in either gist revision.
corrections.caveats: Written for fun to beat the '{n} times faster' benchmark. The author says the technique 'heavily relies on undefined behavior' and 'shouldn't be used for anything other than beating benchmarks'. A helper thread probes past the string in 4 MB steps until it hits SIGSEGV, then memchr runs in parallel over chunks up to the faulting address, so on a real heap with mapped memory after a short string it can scan far beyond the string. The speedup comes from using every online CPU (sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)) against single-threaded libc strlen, not from a better single-thread algorithm. On the same pages the single-thread vector versions do not beat libc: strlen_avx2 7.86 vs 8.76 GB/s on the E5-2650 v4, and strlen_avx2 15.36 and strlen_avx512 16.36 vs 16.84 GB/s on the W-2245. On the W-2245 the byte-loop slow_strlen (while (s[i++] != '\0');) also prints 16.87 GB/s, level with libc, which fits GCC 12+ loop distribution turning the loop into a strlen call or a memory-bandwidth limit (inference, not confirmed). The E5-2650 v4 numbers came from a code version not in the gist (4.00GB, length 4000007776, while both revisions use N_BUF = 2e9). Both gist revisions are dated 2023-07-13; the 2025-12-27 'last active' date does not reflect a code change. The libc and glibc version are not named. No license.

notes: Numbers and the libc strlen baseline are as recorded and the code is public, so tier A holds on the W-2245 run (2.6x, derived from page data). Shortcomings to record: multi-threaded vs single-threaded baseline, UB-based SIGSEGV probing that the author says is for benchmarks only, E5-2650 v4 run from unpublished code, and single-thread AVX2/AVX-512 variants not faster than libc. last_commit corrected to 2023-07-13 (both revisions), which makes it abandoned under the 3-year rule.

tier_reason: The README gives first-party percentage ranges against glibc and other libc memsets, and the benchmark code (bench.c, makefile with -O3 -g -fno-builtin) is public, but no CPU model, compiler version, glibc version or results table is committed, so it stays first-party C.

corrections.workload: bench.c: for each size, 16 warm-up calls, then 100000 calls at each of 64 destination offsets (base malloc+1 plus 0-63), timed with rdtsc/rdtscp around cpuid, fill value 0. main() calls test(64..4100) and bench() subtracts 63, so the measured lengths run from 1 to 4037 bytes, all cache-resident. The output prints each column's time as a ratio to the SSE2 version; no results are committed.
corrections.caveats: Public benchmark code and flags, but no CPU model, compiler version or glibc version, so it falls short of tier A. The 'sys' row is the libc memset reached through -fno-builtin; on glibc the ifunc picks a different variant per CPU, so 'glibc' means different code on different machines. The glibc figure (10-370% for AVX2) has no per-size table, and the author could not force glibc onto its SSE2 path, so the SSE2 version has no glibc figure. The committed bench covers lengths of 1-4037 bytes only, so the README's large-size claims (erms, up to 2x over bionic) are not exercised by it. Ratios are printed relative to the SSE2 version, so AVX2-vs-glibc must be derived. Fill value is always 0, buffers are warm and the same region is hit 100000 times. The README notes that the compiler inlines small constant memsets in real code. The repo describes itself as 'based on microsoft's design'. The competition/ folder vendors bionic, FreeBSD and Solaris memsets. No license file. Last commit 2022-04-05.

notes: README numbers match the record (AVX2 10-370% faster than glibc; SSE2 20-150% vs FreeBSD and 5-100% vs bionic). Shortcomings to record: no CPU, compiler or glibc version, no committed results, the bench covers only 1-4037 bytes with warm cache and fill 0, and no license (reference). Metadata verified: 13 stars, 1 fork, last commit 2022-04-05 (abandoned).

tier_reason: The only number is the README's first-party 'a few cycles' to '7x faster' against the toolchain memmove. The cycle-count harness (common/src/main.c) is public but has no committed results, no CPU core for the 7x and no compiler version, so it stays C.

corrections.baseline: The arm-none-eabi toolchain's newlib-nano memmove: cm4/Makefile and cm0plus/Makefile link with --specs=nano.specs and -fno-builtin. The README calls it 'my standard memmove()' and names no library or version. Newlib's generic memmove.c takes a byte-at-a-time path when built with -Os (__OPTIMIZE_SIZE__), as newlib-nano usually is, which would explain a 7x gap (inference, not confirmed for the author's toolchain).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: arm-none-eabi-gcc (version not stated). Committed Makefiles use -mcpu=cortex-m4 (or the cm0plus equivalent) -mthumb -mfloat-abi=soft --specs=nano.specs -fno-builtin -std=gnu17 -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections, with debug = 1 so OPTIMIZE_FLAGS is -O0 -ggdb3 (-O2 when debug = 0). The flags behind the README claim are not stated. The -O0 setting affects the C harness, not the hand-written assembly or the prebuilt libc memmove.
corrections.workload: common/src/main.c (Greatest tests) times one warm call of each function with the DWT cycle counter after a single untimed call. Sizes are 1, 10, 20 and 50 bytes at source offset 0x81 with destinations 0x7E, 0x82 and 0x102. Slide tests use 15, 21, 34, 512 and 513 bytes against overlapping and non-overlapping destinations. An iterate test up to 35 bytes checks correctness only. Cycle counts are printed over UART and none are committed; the README does not say which size or core gave the 7x.
corrections.caveats: First-party, unqualified range ('a few cycles' to '7x') with no table of cycle counts, sizes or alignments. The baseline is very likely newlib-nano's size-optimised memmove (--specs=nano.specs in both Makefiles), which is a weak incumbent on Cortex-M (byte loop under -Os; inference). The core on which the 7x was measured (M4 versus M0+) is not stated. Committed Makefiles default to debug = 1 (-O0 harness). Each measurement is a single call, so per-call timer overhead matters at 1-50 bytes. A correctness fix ('fixed a bug where we would try to access unaligned memory sometimes', 2025-02-24) landed on the same day as the README update, so the claim may predate it. Very small project (0 stars, 0 forks).

notes: README claim verified as recorded (always faster, a few cycles to 7x, under 230 bytes, GPL-3.0, 0 stars, last commit 2025-02-24, so stale). Shortcomings to record: the baseline is newlib-nano (--specs=nano.specs), a size-optimised incumbent; the 7x has no size, core or table; there are no committed results; and the harness Makefiles default to -O0. A correctness fix for unaligned access landed 2025-02-24.
